thread.title: Bryce Underwood falls short against Texas in Citrus Bowl
thread.title_full: Bryce Underwood falls short against Texas in Citrus Bowl

author: Jonathan Wuchter
title: Bryce Underwood falls short against Texas in Citrus Bowl
text:
ORLANDO, Fla. — Four months ago, freshman quarterback Bryce Underwood played his first game for the now No. 18 Michigan football team. He put together a 251-yard debut in a comfortable 17-point victory.
He graded that performance a “C-plus.” He put the grand expectation on himself to play better and chose to hold himself to a higher standard.
Underwood’s first season officially ended Wednesday. In his 13th game, a concluding Citrus Bowl loss to Texas, Underwood again fell short of his own lofty expectations. While Underwood put up a healthy 199 yards in the air and 77 on the ground, his three second-half turnovers were deserving of a far harsher grade.
“He’s a wonderful kid with a huge upside,” Wolverines interim coach Biff Poggi said. “And he’s a true freshman starting in an elite conference and playing in a bowl game against an SEC football team that was preseason ranked No. 1. I thought he had a great game. He just made a few bad decisions at the end, but he’ll learn. All these things are learning things for him. And so much of playing quarterback is experiential, you know, you have to experience it.”
Much of Michigan’s season has been allowing Underwood to acclimate. The Wolverines’ offensive gameplan in Week 2 against Oklahoma was uber conservative. Against USC, Underwood saw the Trojans’ explosive offense in complete contrast to his own.
But by mid-November, Underwood’s back-to-back 200-yard games suggested Michigan could start to tap into Underwood’s sky-high ceiling. Instead, in a do-or-die meeting with Ohio State, the Wolverines’ game plan wasn’t designed for Underwood to be the decider.
Finally, though, under the interim regime of Poggi and play-calling of tight ends coach Steve Casula in the Citrus Bowl, Underwood was free to go out and show off a year’s worth of development.
“Biff told Casula to just call whatever,” junior running back Bryson Kuzdal said. “And that’s what he did.”
Casula, who called plays in the ReliaQuest Bowl last season, utilized the Wolverines’ young quarterback unlike he had been all season. Underwood’s 42 pass attempts are easily a season high. Wednesday was also the first game all season in which Michigan recorded more passing attempts than rushing attempts. And many of the plays on the ground, 13 to be exact, were with Underwood as the ball carrier, either by design or via his improvisation.
At times Underwood was inspiring in a game without many implications beyond setting up for 2026. For his first touchdown, Underwood placed a ball with impressive touch down the sideline to junior wide receiver Kendrick Bell. Freshman wide receiver Andrew Marsh did most of the work for the second passing touchdown, a pitch and catch to the left flat. But the play showcased the promising Underwood-Marsh connection that the Wolverines’ new coach Kyle Whittingham probably loses sleep hoping to retain.
Underwood was really off the leash on the ground. His 77 yards marked his second highest single-game total this season, sandwiched between Michigan’s wins over Central Michigan and Nebraska — the two other games Poggi served as interim coach for during former coach Sherrone Moore’s suspension. And early in the fourth quarter, an Underwood keeper gave Michigan the 27-24 lead as he dove over a block and just crossed the plane of the end zone before losing control of the ball.
At that point, Underwood’s prowess in the pocket and with his legs made up for his one interception. But after Texas went back to make the game 31-27, Underwood succumbed to his inexperience with two back-breaking interceptions for the Wolverines.
“He’d probably like a couple of those throws back and … (he’s) probably a little down right now,” Poggi said. “But I think the best thing it would be for him is to get back to work as quickly as possible, and for people to remember, he’s just a freshman.”
On third-and-17, the freshman tried to force a ball to Marsh on a corner route. The underneath defender easily read Underwood’s eyes for an interception. A one-play touchdown for Texas quarterback Arch Manning put Underwood fully into desperation mode. On the second play of Michigan’s next drive, Underwood threw an ill-advised ball to an improvising graduate wide receiver Donaven McCulley for his third interception of the day.
A few more hapless heaves in a two-score game were all that followed for Underwood in his freshman finale — and quite possibly, his last game at Michigan. A poor performance, especially in a Bowl Game of all things, is unlikely to dissuade suitors and even more unlikely to dissuade Whittingham from pitching a return. Underwood is still an 18 year old with great potential.
But potential doesn’t erase disappointment. Underwood, who has been hard on himself from day one, didn’t live up to the standard he set. And now, he is no longer a freshman.
